bigQuestion: Does the amount of matter change during a physical change?

sand.title: Where beach sand comes from
vocab: a change that occurs when matter changes form (shape, size) but no new type of matter is formed
text: Sand is made of tiny pieces of rocks and shells. These are broken down by water, wind, and ice. It can take thousands or even millions of years until the pieces are small enough to become sand.

When objects break apart to become sand, no new matter is formed. The materials break into smaller pieces, but they are still the same materials. The rocks and shells have gone through a physical change to create that beautiful beach.
No matter how tiny grains of sand are, they still have the same properties of the material they came from before that material was broken apart.

states.title: Changing state
vocab: the different physical forms of matter — solid, liquid, and gas
text: The different forms, or phases, of matter are called states of matter. Three common states of matter are solids, liquids, and gases.

On a hot day, what happens to ice in your glass of ice water? It melts. When ice melts, it changes from a solid state to a liquid state. Can water change in the opposite way — from a liquid to a solid? Yes! When you make ice, water physically changes state from a liquid to a solid.
When water changes from one phase to another, the amount of water stays the same. But the amount of space the matter is occupying changes.

particles.title: Motion within matter
vocab: matter with definite shape and volume, in which the particles are rigidly arranged in place
matter with definite volume but indefinite shape, in which the particles move around each other freely but do not expand to fill any container
matter with indefinite volume and shape, in which the particles move around freely and expand to fill any container
text: Matter takes the form of a solid, liquid, or gas because of the way the particles are arranged. Because solids keep their own shape, we may conclude that the particles are tightly packed. Solids are rigid, and their particles do not move around each other. Ice, rock, and wood are solids.
Liquids flow and take the shape of whatever container they are in. Because liquids flow, we suspect that the particles can move around each other. Water, milk, and oil are liquids.
In gases, the particles expand to fill their container. Outside of a container, gas particles float apart and spread out in the air.
Particles of matter move more and spread apart as more heat energy is applied to the matter. As more heat is added, solid matter such as glass or steel will melt, as ice does, and become liquid.

dew.title: Puddles and morning dew
vocab: the process involved when matter changes from a liquid to a gas
to change state from gas to liquid
text: When a puddle on a sidewalk dries up, the water in the puddle changes from a liquid to a gas. When the surface of water changes from a liquid to a gas, the process is called evaporation.

Have you ever seen little drops of dew on grass in the morning? Those drops were once water vapor in the air. When the temperature drops, some of the gas condenses, or turns to a liquid, which we see on leaves and grass.

Water changes phases around us every day, but it remains water. Water does not become a different type of matter when it melts in your glass or condenses on grass in your schoolyard. And when water changes physically, the total amount of water before and after the change stays the same.

coins.title: Coin making provides evidence
text: Coins begin their journey to your pocket as long sheets of metal in large, heavy rolls. Little, round discs called blanks are cut from the metal. The scrap metal between the punched-out coins is saved to be recycled.

A nickel weighs 5 grams. Let's suppose that 144 nickels can be made from a sheet of metal. That's a total of 720 grams of nickel coins. But the sheet itself weighs 1,309 grams. What happened to the other 589 grams? That is the scrap left over from stamping the blanks.

If you weighed the coins and scrap together, the total weight would be the same as it was when the metal was an uncut sheet. This is what it means to conserve matter. The weight of matter you start and end with is the same. No matter is gained or lost during a physical change.

casting.title: Casting and crushing
text: Metals can be shaped through a process called casting. Metal is heated until it melts to a liquid state. The molten metal is then poured into a hollow mold, or cast. After the cast cools, the metal has a new shape!

In casting, two physical state changes are used to shape the metal — melting the solid to become molten liquid and then cooling the liquid back to solid forms. The total amount of metal does not change when it changes form. The amount of metal is conserved.

If a can is crushed into a smaller shape, does that mean there is less aluminum inside the recycling bin? Crushing a can is a physical change. When substances undergo physical changes, no matter is gained or lost. The total weight of matter is conserved.

mission.name: Chapter 4 review
mission.blurb: A quick check that the chapter landed — not a test.

items.q: Water, wind, and ice break rocks and shells down into sand over thousands of years. Why does the book call this a physical change?
opts: The rock changes into a brand-new kind of matter that we call sand.
Water, wind, and ice add new material to the rock as they wear it down.
The pieces are smaller, but still made of the same materials.
The grains become far too small for anyone to see them properly.
items.why: "No new matter is formed. The materials break into smaller pieces, but they are still the same materials." A physical change can alter shape and size without making a different substance.

items.q: Water is put in the freezer and turns to ice. What does the book say about the amount of water?
opts: The same water is still there, taking up more space.
Some of the water disappears in the freezer.
New matter is added to the water while it is freezing solid.
There is no way to know unless you weigh the ice afterwards.
items.why: "When water changes from one phase to another, the amount of water stays the same. But the amount of space the matter is occupying changes." Amount and space are two different things.

items.q: Match each word to the meaning the book gives it.
pairs: matter changes form — shape or size — but no new type of matter is made
when matter changes from a liquid to a gas
to change state from a gas to a liquid
the different physical forms — solid, liquid, gas
items.why: These five are Core Vocabulary for this chapter. Every one of them describes a change in form, not a change in how much there is.

items.q: Sort each description into the state of matter it belongs to.
chips: Particles are rigidly arranged in place
Keeps its own shape without a container
Particles move around each other freely
Takes the shape of whatever container it is in
Particles spread out and fill any container
Escapes from an open container into the air
items.why: The book works backwards from what you can see to what the particles must be doing: solids keep their shape, so the particles must be packed tight; liquids flow, so the particles must move past each other; gases spread out, so the particles must be free.

items.q: Which of these show that no matter is lost during a physical change? Select every correct answer.
opts: The coins and the leftover scrap together weigh the same as the uncut sheet
A crushed can holds the same amount of aluminum as before
Metal melted into a mold and cooled is the same amount of metal
A crushed can takes up less space in the recycling bin
Ice floats on top of liquid water
items.why: The last two are true, but neither is about how much matter there is. Taking up less space is a change in shape; floating is about what the water is doing. "The amount of water stays the same. But the amount of space the matter is occupying changes."

items.q: What does the book say happens to particles of matter as more heat energy is added?
opts: They stop moving altogether and lock rigidly into place.
They change into a completely different kind of matter.
They grow heavier and sink towards the bottom.
They move around more and spread further apart.
items.why: "Particles of matter move more and spread apart as more heat energy is applied to the matter." That is why adding enough heat melts a solid — even glass or steel — into a liquid.

items.q: In casting, how many changes of state does the metal go through?
opts: One — the solid metal simply melts and is poured into the mold.
Two — it melts to a liquid, then cools back to a solid.
Three — it passes through solid, then liquid, then gas.
None — casting changes only the shape, never the state.
items.why: "Two physical state changes are used to shape the metal — melting the solid to become molten liquid and then cooling the liquid back to solid forms." The metal ends up a different shape but the same amount.

items.q: There are drops of dew on the grass in the morning, but it did not rain. Where did the water come from?
opts: The grass slowly released water it had been storing in its blades.
The cold night air made brand-new water out of nothing at all.
Water vapor in the air condensed when the temperature dropped.
Water evaporated up out of the soil and settled on the grass.
items.why: "Those drops were once water vapor in the air. When the temperature drops, some of the gas condenses, or turns to a liquid." Nothing new was made — water that was already there changed state.

items.q: Match each piece of evidence to what it shows.

cells: A 1,309 g sheet becomes 720 g of coins and 589 g of scrap
Ice melts in a glass and the water is the same amount
The form changed, the quantity did not
rows.answer: A change of state does not change the amount

cells: A crushed can holds the same aluminum as an uncrushed one
Shape is not the same thing as matter
rows.answer: Shape can change with no matter lost

cells: Metal is melted, poured into a mold, and cooled again
It went one way and came back
rows.answer: Metal can change state and return

choices: A change of state does not change the amount
Shape can change with no matter lost
Metal can change state and return
items.why: Every row is the same idea seen from a different angle: matter can change its shape, its size, or its state, and the amount of it stays exactly the same. That is the chapter's Big Question answered.
